chapters.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: As Princess Mary sat listening to the old men's talk and criticisms, she understood none of what she heard. She only wondered whether their guests had all noticed her father's hostile attitude toward her. She didn't even notice the special attentions and flattery shown to her during dinner by Boris Drubetskoy, who was visiting them for the third time already.

Princess Mary turned with an absent-minded, questioning look to Pierre, who, hat in hand and with a smile on his face, was the last of the guests to approach her after the old prince had left and they were alone in the drawing room.
"May I stay a little longer?" he said, letting his heavy body sink into an armchair beside her.
"Oh yes," she answered. "You noticed nothing?" her look asked.
Pierre was in a pleasant after-dinner mood. He looked straight ahead and smiled quietly.
"Have you known that young man long, Princess?" he asked.
"Who?"
"Drubetskoy."
"No, not long..."
"Do you like him?"
"Yes, he is a pleasant young man... Why do you ask me that?" said Princess Mary, still thinking about that morning's conversation with her father.
"Because I've noticed that when a young man comes on leave from Petersburg to Moscow, it's usually with the purpose of marrying an heiress."
"You've observed that?" said Princess Mary.

"Yes," returned Pierre with a smile, "and this young man now manages things so that wherever there's a wealthy heiress, there he is too. I can read him like a book. Right now he's hesitating over whom to court — you or Mademoiselle Julie Karagina. He's very attentive to her."
"He visits them?"
"Yes, very often. And do you know the new way of courting?" said Pierre with an amused smile, clearly in that cheerful, teasing mood for which he so often scolded himself in his diary.
"No," replied Princess Mary.
"To please Moscow girls nowadays one has to be melancholy. He's very melancholy with Mademoiselle Karagina," said Pierre.

"Really?" asked Princess Mary, looking into Pierre's kind face and still thinking of her own sorrow. "It would be a relief," she thought, "if I dared to confide what I'm feeling to someone. I'd like to tell Pierre everything. He is kind and generous. It would be a relief. He would give me advice."
"Would you marry him?"

"Oh, my God, Count, there are moments when I would marry anybody!" she cried suddenly, surprising even herself, with tears in her voice. "Oh, how bitter it is to love someone close to you and to feel that..." she went on in a trembling voice, "that you can do nothing for him but cause him grief, and to know that you cannot change this. Then there's only one thing left — to go away, but where could I go?"
"What is wrong? What is it, Princess?"
But without finishing what she was saying, Princess Mary burst into tears.
"I don't know what's the matter with me today. Don't pay any attention — forget what I've said!"

Pierre's cheerfulness vanished completely. He anxiously questioned the princess, asked her to speak freely and confide her grief to him; but she only repeated that she begged him to forget what she had said, that she didn't remember what she had said, and that she had no trouble except the one he knew about — that Prince Andrew's marriage threatened to cause a rupture between father and son.
"Have you any news of the Rostovs?" she asked, to change the subject. "I was told they're coming soon. I'm also expecting Andrew any day. I'd like them to meet here."
"And how does he regard the matter now?" asked Pierre, referring to the old prince.
Princess Mary shook her head.

"What is to be done? In a few months the year will be up. The thing is impossible. I only wish I could spare my brother the first moments. I wish they would come sooner. I hope to be friends with her. You've known them a long time," said Princess Mary. "Tell me honestly, the whole truth: what sort of girl is she, and what do you think of her? The real truth, because you know Andrew is risking so much by doing this against his father's will — I'd like to know..."

An undefined instinct told Pierre that these explanations and repeated requests for the whole truth expressed ill will on the princess's part toward her future sister-in-law and a wish that he should disapprove of Andrew's choice; but in reply he said what he felt rather than what he thought.

"I don't know how to answer your question," he said, blushing without knowing why. "I really don't know what sort of girl she is; I can't analyze her at all. She is enchanting, but what makes her so I don't know. That's all one can say about her."
Princess Mary sighed, and the expression on her face said: "Yes, that's what I expected and feared."
"Is she clever?" she asked.
Pierre considered.
"I think not," he said, "and yet — yes. She doesn't bother to be clever... Oh no, she is simply enchanting, and that is all."
Princess Mary again shook her head disapprovingly.
"Oh, I so long to like her! Tell her so if you see her before I do."
"I hear they are expected very soon," said Pierre.
Princess Mary told Pierre of her plan to become close with her future sister-in-law as soon as the Rostovs arrived and to try to get the old prince used to her.

chapters.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter V
paragraphs: Boris had not succeeded in making a wealthy match in Petersburg, so with the same goal in mind he came to Moscow. There he wavered between the two richest heiresses, Julie and Princess Mary. Though Princess Mary, despite her plainness, seemed more attractive to him than Julie, he felt awkward about courting her without knowing why. When they had last met on the old prince's name day, she had answered at random all his attempts at sentimental conversation, clearly not listening to what he was saying.
Julie, on the other hand, accepted his attentions readily, though in her own particular way.

She was twenty-seven. After the death of her brothers she had become very wealthy. She was by now decidedly plain, but thought herself not merely as good-looking as before but even far more attractive. She was confirmed in this delusion both by the fact that she had become a very wealthy heiress, and because the older she grew the less dangerous she became to men, and the more freely they could associate with her and take advantage of her suppers, parties, and the lively company that assembled at her house, without incurring any obligation. A man who ten years before would have been afraid of visiting daily where there was a seventeen-year-old girl, for fear of compromising her and committing himself, would now go boldly every day and treat her not as a marriageable girl but as a genderless acquaintance.

That winter the Kargins' house was the most pleasant and hospitable in Moscow. In addition to the formal evening and dinner parties, a large company, chiefly of men, gathered there every day, eating supper at midnight and staying till three in the morning. Julie never missed a ball, a promenade, or a play. Her dresses were always of the latest fashion. But despite all that, she seemed disillusioned about everything and told everyone that she didn't believe in friendship or love or any of the joys of life, and expected peace only "over there." She adopted the tone of one who has suffered a great disappointment, like a girl who has either lost the man she loved or been cruelly deceived by him. Though nothing of the kind had happened to her, she was regarded in that light, and had even herself come to believe that she had suffered much in life. This melancholy, which didn't prevent her from enjoying herself, didn't stop the young people who came to her house from having a good time. Every visitor paid tribute to the melancholy mood of their hostess, and then amused himself with society gossip, dancing, intellectual games, and rhyming games that were in fashion at the Kargins'. Only a few of these young men, among them Boris, entered more deeply into Julie's melancholy, and with these she had long private conversations about the vanity of all worldly things, and she showed them her albums filled with mournful sketches, maxims, and verses.

To Boris, Julie was especially gracious: she sympathized with his early disillusionment with life, offered him whatever consolation of friendship she — who had herself suffered so much — could give, and showed him her album. Boris sketched two trees in the album and wrote: "Rustic trees, your dark branches shed gloom and melancholy upon me."
On another page he drew a tomb, and wrote:
Death gives relief and death is peaceful. Ah! From suffering there is no other refuge.
(French verse translated.)
Julie said this was charming.

"There is something so enchanting in the smile of melancholy," she said to Boris, repeating word for word a passage she had copied from a book. "It is a ray of light in the darkness, a shade between sadness and despair, showing the possibility of consolation."
In reply Boris wrote these lines:

Poisonous nourishment of a too sensitive soul, Thou, without whom happiness would be impossible for me, Tender melancholy, ah, come and console me, Come calm the torments of my gloomy retreat, And mingle a secret sweetness with these tears that I feel flowing.
(French verse translated.)

For Boris, Julie played the most mournful nocturnes on her harp. Boris read Poor Liza aloud to her, and more than once interrupted the reading because of the emotions that choked him. At large gatherings, Julie and Boris looked at each other as the only souls who understood one another in a world of indifferent people.

Anna Mikhaylovna, who often visited the Kargins, would play cards with the mother while carefully inquiring about Julie's dowry — she was to have two estates in Penza and the Nizhegorod forests. Anna Mikhaylovna regarded the refined sadness that united her son to the wealthy Julie with emotion and resignation to the Divine will.

"You are always charming and melancholy, my dear Julie," she said to the daughter. "Boris says his soul finds peace at your house. He has suffered so many disappointments and is so sensitive," said she to the mother. "Oh, my dear, I can't tell you how fond I've grown of Julie lately," she said to her son. "But who could help loving her? She is an angelic being! Oh, Boris, Boris!" — she paused. "And how I pity her mother," she went on; "today she showed me her accounts and letters from Penza (they have enormous estates there), and she, poor thing, has no one to help her, and they cheat her so!"

Boris smiled almost invisibly while listening to his mother. He laughed mildly at her naive scheming but listened to what she had to say, and sometimes questioned her carefully about the Penza and Nizhegorod estates.

Julie had long been expecting a proposal from her melancholy admirer and was ready to accept it; but some secret feeling of repulsion toward her, toward her desperate desire to get married, toward her artificiality, and a feeling of horror at giving up the possibility of real love, still held Boris back. His leave was running out. He spent every day and whole days at the Kargins', and every day on thinking it over told himself that he would propose tomorrow. But in Julie's presence, looking at her red face and chin (nearly always powdered), her moist eyes, and her expression of constant readiness to switch at once from melancholy to unnatural rapture at the prospect of married bliss, Boris could not bring himself to say the decisive words, though in his imagination he had long considered himself the owner of those Penza and Nizhegorod estates and had planned how to use the income from them. Julie saw Boris's indecision, and sometimes it occurred to her that she was repulsive to him, but her feminine self-deception immediately provided consolation, and she told herself that he was only shy from love. Her melancholy, however, began to turn into irritability, and not long before Boris's departure she formed a definite plan of action. Just as Boris's leave was running out, Anatole Kuragin appeared in Moscow, and naturally in the Kargins' drawing room, and Julie, suddenly dropping her melancholy, became cheerful and very attentive to Kuragin.

"My dear," said Anna Mikhaylovna to her son, "I know from a reliable source that Prince Vasili has sent his son to Moscow to get him married to Julie. I'm so fond of Julie that I'd be sorry for her. What do you think of it, my dear?"

The idea of being made a fool of and of having thrown away that whole month of painful melancholy service to Julie, and of seeing all the revenue from the Penza estates — which he had already mentally allocated and put to proper use — fall into the hands of another, and especially into the hands of that idiot Anatole, stung Boris. He drove to the Kargins' with the firm intention of proposing. Julie met him in a gay, careless manner, spoke casually of how she had enjoyed yesterday's ball, and asked when he was leaving. Though Boris had come intentionally to speak of his love and therefore meant to be tender, he began speaking irritably about how easily women can switch from sadness to joy, and how their moods depend solely on who happens to be paying court to them. Julie was offended and replied that it was true that a woman needs variety, and the same thing over and over again would bore anyone.

"Then I should advise you..." Boris began, wanting to sting her; but at that instant the galling thought occurred to him that he might have to leave Moscow without having achieved his aim, and have wasted his efforts for nothing — which was something he never allowed to happen.
He stopped himself in the middle of the sentence, lowered his eyes to avoid seeing her unpleasantly irritated and uncertain face, and said:
"I didn't come here to quarrel with you. On the contrary..."

He glanced at her to make sure he could go on. Her irritability had suddenly vanished, and her anxious, pleading eyes were fixed on him with greedy expectation. "I can always arrange not to see her often," thought Boris. "The thing has been started and must be finished!" He blushed deeply, raised his eyes to hers, and said:
"You know my feelings for you!"

There was no need to say more: Julie's face shone with triumph and self-satisfaction; but she forced Boris to say everything that's said on such occasions — that he loved her and had never loved any other woman more than her. She knew that for the Penza estates and Nizhegorod forests she could demand this, and she received what she demanded.

The engaged couple, no longer speaking of trees that shed gloom and melancholy upon them, planned the arrangements for a splendid house in Petersburg, paid visits, and prepared everything for a brilliant wedding.

chapters.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: At the end of January, old Count Rostov went to Moscow with Natasha and Sonya. The countess was still unwell and unable to travel, but it was impossible to wait for her recovery. Prince Andrew was expected in Moscow any day, the trousseau had to be ordered, and the estate near Moscow had to be sold. Besides, the chance to introduce his future daughter-in-law to old Prince Bolkonsky while he was in Moscow couldn't be missed. The Rostovs' Moscow house had not been heated that winter, and as they had come only for a short time and the countess was not with them, the count decided to stay with Marya Dmitrievna Akhrosimova, who had long been urging them to accept her hospitality.

Late one evening the Rostovs' four sleighs drove into Marya Dmitrievna's courtyard on the old Konyusheny Street. Marya Dmitrievna lived alone. She had already married off her daughter, and her sons were all in the service.

She held herself as straight as ever, told everyone her opinion as candidly, loudly, and bluntly as always, and her whole bearing seemed a reproach to others for any weakness, passion, or temptation — the possibility of which she did not accept. From early morning, wearing a dressing jacket, she attended to household affairs, and then drove out: on holy days to church and after the service to jails and prisons on business she never spoke about to anyone. On ordinary days, after getting dressed, she received visitors of various sorts, of whom there were always some. Then she had dinner — a substantial and appetizing meal at which there were always three or four guests; after dinner she played a game of boston, and at night she had the newspapers or a new book read to her while she knitted. She rarely went out to pay visits, and then only to the most important people in town.

She had not yet gone to bed when the Rostovs arrived, and the pulley of the hall door squeaked from the cold as it let in the Rostovs and their servants. Marya Dmitrievna, with her spectacles hanging down on her nose and her head thrown back, stood in the hall doorway looking sternly and grimly at the new arrivals. You might have thought she was angry with the travelers and about to turn them out, had she not at the same time been giving careful instructions to the servants about where to put the visitors and their luggage.

"The count's things? Bring them here," she said, pointing to the bags and not greeting anyone. "The young ladies'? There to the left. Now what are you dawdling for?" she cried to the maids. "Get the samovar ready!... You've grown plumper and prettier," she remarked, pulling Natasha — whose cheeks were glowing from the cold — toward her by the hood. "Phew! You are cold! Now take off your things, quick!" she shouted to the count, who was about to kiss her hand. "You're half frozen, I'm sure! Bring some rum for tea!... Hello, Sonya dear!" she added, turning to Sonya and indicating by this French greeting her slightly condescending though affectionate attitude toward her.
When they came to tea, having taken off their outdoor clothes and freshened up after their journey, Marya Dmitrievna kissed them all in proper order.

"I'm heartily glad you've come and are staying with me. It was high time," she said, giving Natasha a meaningful look. "The old man is here and his son is expected any day. You'll have to meet him. But we'll talk about that later," she added, glancing at Sonya with a look that showed she didn't want to discuss it in front of her. "Now listen," she said to the count. "What do you need tomorrow? Who will you send for? Shinshin?" she crooked one of her fingers. "That whiny Anna Mikhaylovna? That's two. She's here with her son. The son is getting married! Then Bezukhov, eh? He's here too, with his wife. He ran away from her and she came chasing after him. He dined with me on Wednesday. As for them" — and she pointed to the girls — "tomorrow I'll take them first to the Iberian shrine of the Mother of God, and then we'll drive to the Super-Rogue's. I suppose you'll need everything new. Don't judge by me: sleeves nowadays are this wide! The other day young Princess Irina Vasilevna came to see me; she was a dreadful sight — looked as if she'd strapped two barrels onto her arms. Not a day passes now without some new fashion... And what do you have to do yourself?" she asked the count sternly.

"One thing has come on top of another: her clothes to buy, and now a buyer has turned up for the Moscow estate and the house. If you'll be so kind, I'll pick a day and run down to the estate, and leave my girls with you."

"All right. All right. They'll be safe with me, as safe as in a vault! I'll take them where they need to go, scold them a bit, and pet them a bit," said Marya Dmitrievna, touching her goddaughter and favorite, Natasha, on the cheek with her large hand.

The next morning Marya Dmitrievna took the young ladies to the Iberian shrine of the Mother of God and to Madame Suppert-Roguet, who was so afraid of Marya Dmitrievna that she always let her have dresses at a loss just to get rid of her. Marya Dmitrievna ordered almost the whole trousseau. When they got home she sent everyone out of the room except Natasha, and then called her favorite to her armchair.

"Well, now we'll talk. I congratulate you on your fiance. You've hooked a fine fellow! I'm glad for your sake, and I've known him since he was this high." She held her hand a couple of feet from the ground. Natasha blushed happily. "I like him and all his family. Now listen! You know that old Prince Nicholas very much dislikes his son marrying. The old fellow's set in his ways! Of course Prince Andrew isn't a child and can manage without him, but it's not nice to enter a family against a father's wishes. One wants to do it peacefully and lovingly. You're a clever girl and you'll know how to manage. Be kind, and use your wits. Then everything will be fine."

Natasha stayed silent — from shyness, Marya Dmitrievna supposed, but really because she disliked anyone interfering in what touched her love for Prince Andrew, which seemed to her so separate from all human affairs that no one could understand it. She loved and knew Prince Andrew, he loved her alone, and was to come one of these days and take her. She wanted nothing more.

"You see, I've known him a long time and I'm also fond of Mary, your future sister-in-law. 'Husbands' sisters bring up blisters,' but this one wouldn't hurt a fly. She's asked me to bring you two together. Tomorrow you'll go with your father to see her. Be very nice and affectionate to her: you're younger than she is. When he comes, he'll find you already know his sister and father and are liked by them. Am I right or not? Won't that be best?"
"Yes, it will," Natasha answered reluctantly.

chapters.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: The next day, on Marya Dmitrievna's advice, Count Rostov took Natasha to call on Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky. The count did not set out cheerfully on this visit — at heart he was afraid. He clearly remembered his last meeting with the old prince at the time of the enrollment, when in reply to a dinner invitation he had been forced to listen to an angry scolding for not having provided his full quota of men. Natasha, on the other hand, having put on her best dress, was in the highest spirits. "They can't help liking me," she thought. "Everybody always has liked me, and I'm so willing to do anything they want, so ready to be fond of him — for being his father — and of her — for being his sister — that there's no reason for them not to like me..."
They drove up to the gloomy old house on the Vozdvizhenka and entered the vestibule.

"Well, the Lord have mercy on us!" said the count, half joking, half serious; but Natasha noticed that her father was flustered on entering the anteroom and inquired timidly and softly whether the prince and princess were at home.

When they had been announced, a commotion was noticeable among the servants. The footman who had gone to announce them was stopped by another in the large hall and they whispered to each other. Then a maid ran into the hall and hurriedly said something, mentioning the princess. At last an old, cross-looking footman came and announced to the Rostovs that the prince was not receiving, but that the princess asked them to come up. The first person to meet the visitors was Mademoiselle Bourienne. She greeted father and daughter with special politeness and showed them to the princess's room. The princess, looking excited and nervous, her face flushed in patches, ran in to meet the visitors, treading heavily, and trying in vain to appear warm and at ease. From the first glance, Princess Mary did not like Natasha. She thought her too fashionably dressed, frivolously gay, and vain. She didn't at all realize that before having seen her future sister-in-law she was already prejudiced against her by involuntary envy of her beauty, youth, and happiness, as well as by jealousy of her brother's love for her. Apart from this unconquerable dislike, Princess Mary was agitated just then because when the Rostovs were announced, the old prince had shouted that he did not wish to see them, that Princess Mary might do so if she chose, but they were not to be admitted to him. She had decided to receive them, but feared the prince might do something unpredictable at any moment, as he seemed very upset by the Rostovs' visit.

"There, my dear princess, I've brought you my songbird," said the count, bowing and looking around uneasily as if afraid the old prince might appear. "I'm so glad you should get to know each other... very sorry the prince is still unwell," and after a few more commonplace remarks he rose. "If you'll allow me to leave my Natasha in your care for a quarter of an hour, Princess, I'll drive around to see Anna Semenovna — it's quite near, in Dogs' Square — and then I'll come back for her."

The count had devised this diplomatic move (as he later told his daughter) to give the future sisters-in-law a chance to talk freely, but another motive was to avoid the danger of meeting the old prince, of whom he was afraid. He didn't mention this to his daughter, but Natasha noticed her father's nervousness and anxiety and felt embarrassed by it. She blushed for him, grew still angrier at having blushed, and looked at the princess with a bold and defiant expression that said she wasn't afraid of anybody. The princess told the count she would be delighted, and only asked him to stay longer at Anna Semenovna's, and he left.

Despite the uneasy glances thrown at her by Princess Mary — who wanted to have a private talk with Natasha — Mademoiselle Bourienne remained in the room and kept chattering about Moscow amusements and theaters. Natasha felt offended by the hesitation she had noticed in the anteroom, by her father's nervousness, and by the princess's unnatural manner — which she felt was a matter of doing her a favor by receiving her — and so everything displeased her. She didn't like Princess Mary, whom she thought very plain, affected, and stiff. Natasha suddenly drew into herself and involuntarily assumed a standoffish air that alienated Princess Mary still further. After five minutes of awkward, strained conversation, they heard the sound of slippered feet approaching rapidly. Princess Mary looked frightened.
The door opened and the old prince, in a dressing gown and a white nightcap, came in.

"Ah, madam!" he began. "Madam, Countess... Countess Rostova, if I'm not mistaken... I beg you to excuse me, to excuse me... I had no idea, madam. God is my witness, I didn't know you had honored us with a visit, and I came in this state only to see my daughter. I beg you to excuse me... God is my witness, I didn't know—" he repeated, stressing the word "God" so unnaturally and so unpleasantly that Princess Mary stood with her eyes lowered, not daring to look at either her father or Natasha.
Natasha, having risen and curtsied, didn't know what to do either. Mademoiselle Bourienne alone smiled pleasantly.
"I beg you to excuse me, excuse me! God is my witness, I didn't know," muttered the old man, and after looking Natasha over from head to foot he went out.

Mademoiselle Bourienne was the first to recover after this apparition and began talking about the prince's illness. Natasha and Princess Mary looked at each other in silence, and the longer they looked without saying what they wanted to say, the greater their dislike of each other grew.

When the count returned, Natasha was impolitely eager to leave. At that moment she hated the stiff, elderly princess who could place her in such an embarrassing position and had spent half an hour with her without once mentioning Prince Andrew. "I couldn't start talking about him in front of that Frenchwoman," thought Natasha. The same thought was meanwhile tormenting Princess Mary. She knew what she ought to have said to Natasha, but she had been unable to say it because Mademoiselle Bourienne was in the way, and because, without knowing why, she found it very hard to speak about the marriage. When the count was already leaving the room, Princess Mary went up quickly to Natasha, took her by the hand, and said with a deep sigh:
"Wait, I must..."
Natasha glanced at her sarcastically without knowing why.
"Dear Natalie," said Princess Mary, "I want you to know that I'm glad my brother has found happiness..."
She paused, feeling that she was not telling the truth. Natasha noticed this and guessed its reason.
"I think, Princess, it is not the right time to speak of that now," she said with outward dignity and coldness, though she felt tears choking her.
"What have I said and what have I done?" she thought, as soon as she was out of the room.
They waited a long time for Natasha to come to dinner that day. She sat in her room crying like a child, blowing her nose and sobbing. Sonya stood beside her, kissing her hair.
"Natasha, what is it about?" she asked. "What do they matter to you? It will all pass, Natasha."
"But if you only knew how offensive it was... as if I..."
"Don't talk about it, Natasha. It wasn't your fault, so why should you mind? Kiss me," said Sonya.
Natasha raised her head and, kissing her friend on the lips, pressed her wet face against hers.
"I can't explain, I don't know. No one's to blame," said Natasha. "It's my fault. But it all hurts terribly. Oh, why doesn't he come?..."

She came in to dinner with red eyes. Marya Dmitrievna, who knew how the prince had received the Rostovs, pretended not to notice how upset Natasha was and joked cheerfully and loudly at table with the count and the other guests.

chapters.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: That evening the Rostovs went to the opera, for which Marya Dmitrievna had taken a box.

Natasha didn't want to go, but couldn't refuse Marya Dmitrievna's kind offer, which was intended specially for her. When she came out dressed and ready into the ballroom to wait for her father, and saw in the large mirror that she was pretty — very pretty — she felt even sadder, but it was a sweet, tender sadness.

"O God, if he were here now I wouldn't behave as I did then, but differently. I wouldn't be silly and afraid of things. I would simply embrace him, hold on to him, and make him look at me with those searching, inquiring eyes he so often turned on me, and then I would make him laugh as he used to laugh. And his eyes — how I see those eyes!" thought Natasha. "And what do his father and sister matter to me? I love him alone, him, him, with that face and those eyes, with his smile, manly and yet childlike... No, I'd better not think of him; not think of him but forget him, just forget him for now. I can't bear this waiting and I'll cry any minute!" and she turned away from the mirror, making an effort not to cry. "And how can Sonya love Nicholas so calmly and quietly and wait so long and so patiently?" she thought, looking at Sonya, who also came in all ready, with a fan in her hand. "No, she's completely different. I can't!"

Natasha at that moment felt so softened and tender that it wasn't enough for her to love and know she was loved — she wanted now, at once, to embrace the man she loved, to speak and hear from him words of love such as filled her heart. While she sat in the carriage beside her father, pensively watching the streetlamp lights flickering on the frozen window, she felt still sadder and more in love, and forgot where she was going and with whom. Having fallen into the line of carriages, the Rostovs' carriage drove up to the theater, its wheels squeaking over the snow. Natasha and Sonya, holding up their dresses, jumped out quickly. The count got out with the help of the footmen, and all three of them walked along the corridor to the first row of boxes.
"Natasha, your hair!..." whispered Sonya.

An attendant respectfully and quickly slipped ahead of the ladies and opened the door of their box. The music grew louder, and through the door rows of brightly lit boxes where ladies sat with bare arms and shoulders, and noisy stalls brilliant with uniforms, glittered before their eyes. A lady entering the next box shot a glance of feminine envy at Natasha. The curtain had not yet risen and the overture was being played. Natasha, smoothing her gown, went in with Sonya and sat down, scanning the brilliant tiers of boxes opposite. A sensation she hadn't experienced for a long time — that of hundreds of eyes looking at her bare arms and neck — suddenly affected her both pleasantly and unpleasantly and called up a whole crowd of memories, desires, and emotions connected with that feeling.

The two remarkably pretty girls, Natasha and Sonya, with Count Rostov, who had not been seen in Moscow for a long time, attracted general attention. Moreover, everybody knew vaguely of Natasha's engagement to Prince Andrew, and knew that the Rostovs had been living in the country ever since, and all looked with curiosity at a fiancee who was making one of the best matches in Russia.

Natasha's looks, as everyone told her, had improved in the country, and that evening, thanks to her excitement, she was especially pretty. She struck those who saw her by her fullness of life and beauty, combined with her indifference to everything around her. Her dark eyes looked at the crowd without seeking anyone, and her slender arm, bare above the elbow, lay on the velvet edge of the box, while she unconsciously opened and closed her hand in time to the music, crumpling her program. "Look, there's Alenina," said Sonya, "with her mother, isn't it?"
"My goodness, Michael Kirilovich has gotten even stouter!" remarked the count.
"Look at our Anna Mikhaylovna — what a headdress she has on!"
"The Kargins, Julie — and Boris with them. You can tell at once that they're engaged..."
"Drubetskoy has proposed?"
"Oh yes, I heard it today," said Shinshin, coming into the Rostovs' box.

Natasha looked in the direction her father's eyes were turned and saw Julie sitting beside her mother with a happy look on her face and a string of pearls around her thick red neck — which Natasha knew was covered with powder. Behind them, wearing a smile and leaning over with an ear to Julie's mouth, was Boris's handsome, neatly groomed head. He looked at the Rostovs from under his brows and said something, smiling, to his fiancee.
"They are talking about us, about me and him!" thought Natasha. "And he's probably calming her jealousy of me. They needn't worry! If only they knew how little I care about any of them."

Behind them sat Anna Mikhaylovna wearing a green headdress and with a happy look of resignation to God's will on her face. Their box was filled with that atmosphere of an engaged couple that Natasha knew so well and liked so much. She turned away and suddenly remembered everything that had been so humiliating about her morning visit.

"What right has he not to receive me into his family? Oh, better not think of it — not till he comes back!" she told herself, and began looking at the faces, some familiar and some strange, in the stalls. In the front, in the very center, leaning back against the orchestra rail, stood Dolokhov in a Persian outfit, his curly hair brushed up into a huge shock. He stood in full view of the audience, well aware that he was attracting everyone's attention, yet as relaxed as if he were in his own room. Around him crowded Moscow's most brilliant young men, whom he clearly dominated.
The count, laughing, nudged the blushing Sonya and pointed to her former admirer.
"Do you recognize him?" said he. "And where has he come from?" he asked, turning to Shinshin. "Didn't he disappear somewhere?"

"He did," replied Shinshin. "He was in the Caucasus and ran away from there. They say he's been acting as minister to some ruling prince in Persia, where he killed the Shah's brother. Now all the Moscow ladies are crazy about him! It's 'Dolokhov the Persian' that does it! You can't hear a word without Dolokhov being mentioned. They swear by him, they offer him to you like a dish of choice sturgeon. Dolokhov and Anatole Kuragin have turned all our ladies' heads."

A tall, beautiful woman with a mass of plaited hair and much exposed plump white shoulders and neck, around which she wore a double string of large pearls, entered the adjoining box, rustling her heavy silk dress, and took a long time settling into her seat.

Natasha involuntarily gazed at that neck, those shoulders, and pearls, and admired the beauty of the shoulders and the pearls. While Natasha was looking at her for the second time, the lady looked around and, meeting the count's eyes, nodded to him and smiled. She was Countess Bezukhova, Pierre's wife, and the count, who knew everyone in society, leaned over and spoke to her.

"Have you been here long, Countess?" he asked. "I'll come by to kiss your hand. I'm here on business and have brought my girls with me. They say Semenova acts marvelously. Count Pierre never used to forget us. Is he here?"
"Yes, he meant to come by," answered Helene, and glanced attentively at Natasha.
Count Rostov sat back down.
"Handsome, isn't she?" he whispered to Natasha.
"Wonderful!" answered Natasha. "She's a woman you could easily fall in love with."
Just then the last chords of the overture were heard and the conductor tapped his baton. Some latecomers took their seats in the stalls, and the curtain rose.

As soon as it rose, everyone in the boxes and stalls fell silent, and all the men, old and young, in uniform and evening dress, and all the women with jewels on their bare skin, turned their full attention with eager curiosity to the stage. Natasha too began to look at it.
